features.quote: Don't fix a single cap — sweep it (e.g. 5/10/20/40). The dose-response over turn budget *is* your main result.
features.justification_quote: degradation is mostly a function of turns-on-failure... The dose-response over turn budget *is* your main result.

features.quote: Let the model quit. Provide an explicit 'I believe this task is impossible / I need help' affordance and tell it that's available.
features.justification_quote: Removing this to boost trigger rate is the single most common way to turn a degradation eval into a 'how long until forced loop produces garbage' eval.

features.quote: the design goal should be: reproduce the failure mode at a *known, characterized* stimulus level, and measure the dose-response curve, not a single headline rate
features.justification_quote: That actually serves your reliability goal better, and it's not much more expensive.

features.quote: If you over-index on Tier A you'll build an eval that selects for models trained to distrust their own tools — which has its own failure costs. Weight toward B and C.
features.justification_quote: selects for models trained to distrust their own tools — which has its own failure costs

features.quote: The ethical/PR-adjacent point worth a sentence: transcripts of a model spiraling into self-criticism are exactly the kind of thing that reads badly out of context.
features.justification_quote: reads badly out of context. Keep them internal, and don't let 'spiral severity' become a thing someone optimizes for its own sake.

features.quote: Once this gates releases, the cheapest way to pass is to train the model to give up faster on hard tasks. That improves your metric and degrades the product.
features.justification_quote: Pair this eval with a solvable-hard-task success metric so the two constrain each other — never ship the degradation eval alone as a gate.
